title: We Walk by Faith, Not by Sight
speaker: Jonathan Baird
summary: The cares of this world squeeze out everything heavenly. But a Christian is oriented to the unseen, longs to be with the Lord, and aims to please him.
exhortation: Do we walk by faith? Do we really? The cares of this world so easily muscle in on everything spiritual. At least that's how it seems to work in my life. Everything heavenly, everything focused on Christ, gets squeezed out so easily that we don't live by faith. We actually live by sight. We look around at the world and see material wealth, and even if we wouldn't say it out loud, we orient our lives around the visible.

But Paul makes it clear that the orientation of the Christian is completely different from the natural world. Apart from Christ, this material world is it. What you see is what you get. But that's not our faith. We hope in what is unseen and eternal. To be at home in the body is to be away from the Lord, so we long to be with our Savior and King, Jesus. And for a Christian, to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord. What an encouraging thought about the saints who have gone before us: they are with him, living in the joy of their Savior's company.

So what does that mean for us today? It means we must make it our aim to please the Lord, because the day is coming soon when we will all appear before the judgment seat of Christ. Believe that. Each of us will receive what is due. So, Lord, may we live our lives before your face, with your glory, your kingdom and your purposes highest in our lives.
prayer: Lord, what a wonderful promise we have. Thank you for opening our eyes to who you are and to the glorious future we have in you. Fill us with faith, so that we have eyes of faith as we look out on the world and the day ahead, and see rightly.

Remind us of the promises we have in you, and that you never break a promise. Thank you for your wonderful grace, by which we can be sure that you are with us and will fulfill every promise you've made. In Jesus' name.
